title: Non-Fiction Text Types & Analysis
description: Understanding articles, speeches, letters, biographies, travel writing, reviews, and how non-fiction authors achieve their purpose.

notes.heading: Types of Non-Fiction Texts
notes.body: Non-fiction encompasses many genres: News article (objective reporting of events — inverted pyramid: most important first), Feature article (in-depth exploration — more stylistic, narrative elements), Editorial/opinion piece (argues a position), Speech (written to be spoken aloud — rhetorical devices prominent), Biography/autobiography (life story — autobiography = self-written), Memoir (personal reflection on specific period/theme), Travel writing (descriptive + reflective), Review (critique of book/film/performance — informed opinion), Essay (personal reflection or academic argument), Letter (formal or personal correspondence), Diary/journal (intimate, chronological record), Blog (informal, personal voice, often interactive). Each text type has conventions (expected features) — understanding conventions helps you analyse how authors work within or subvert them.

notes.heading: Analysing Non-Fiction: Purpose and Audience
notes.body: Every non-fiction text has a purpose and intended audience. Ask: Who is this written for? What does the author want the reader to think/feel/do? How do language, structure, and content choices reflect the target audience? A scientific article for specialists uses technical jargon; a popular science article for general readers uses analogies and avoids jargon. A tabloid newspaper uses short sentences, emotive language, and sensationalism; a broadsheet uses measured tone and detailed analysis. When analysing, let the audience and purpose guide your interpretation of authorial choices.

notes.heading: Bias, Objectivity and Perspective
notes.body: No text is perfectly objective — every author has a perspective. Bias in non-fiction: selection of facts (what's included/excluded), framing (how events are presented), language choices (loaded vs neutral), sources quoted (which voices are heard/absent). Critical readers: (1) Identify the author's perspective. (2) Consider what perspective is missing. (3) Distinguish fact from opinion. (4) Evaluate the credibility of sources. Objectivity is an ideal (especially in journalism and science writing), but awareness of inevitable subjectivity is essential. Good non-fiction writing acknowledges limitations and may explicitly state its perspective rather than pretending to neutrality.

notes.heading: Language Features in Non-Fiction
notes.body: Non-fiction uses many of the same techniques as fiction and persuasive writing, applied differently: Anecdotes — humanise abstract topics. Statistics/data — establish authority, build logical case. Expert quotation — borrow credibility. Imagery/description — make abstract concrete (travel writing, features). Metaphor/analogy — explain complex ideas (science writing). Rhetorical questions — engage reader in argument. Direct address — create personal connection. Tone — formal, conversational, urgent, reflective — shifts to match purpose. Headings and subheadings — guide reader, break text, create emphasis. Captions and pull quotes — highlight key information. Text structure: compare-contrast, problem-solution, chronological, thematic.

notes.heading: Speeches and Spoken Text Analysis
notes.body: Speeches are written to be heard, not just read. Features: Direct address to audience ('My friends,' 'Fellow citizens'). Rhetorical devices amplified for oral delivery — repetition and tricolon create rhythm when spoken. Pacing indicated by sentence length and punctuation. Tone shifts signalled by word choice. Anecdotes personalise abstract arguments. Call and response elements (explicit or implied). Memorable phrasing: sound devices (alliteration, assonance) aid memory when spoken. Analysing speeches: what is the occasion? Who is the audience? What does the speaker want? How do delivery features (volume, pace, pauses — implied by punctuation and structure) support the message?

notes.heading: Reviews: Evaluating and Critiquing
notes.body: A review is both informative and evaluative. It should: (1) Provide context (what is being reviewed, basic plot/premise without spoilers). (2) Analyse elements (for a film: acting, direction, cinematography, script; for a book: characterisation, plot, style, themes). (3) Support opinions with specific examples. (4) Conclude with a clear recommendation. Strong reviews: avoid simple 'good/bad' judgments, explain WHY something works or doesn't, consider the work on its own terms (is it achieving what it sets out to do?), acknowledge personal taste while striving for fair assessment. Weak reviews: purely subjective ('I liked it'), purely descriptive summary, lacking evidence, overly harsh or gushing without justification.

notes.heading: Comparing Non-Fiction Texts
notes.body: Comparative analysis of non-fiction examines: How do two texts on the same topic differ? Consider: purpose (to inform vs to persuade), audience (specialist vs general), tone (objective vs emotional), evidence (statistics vs anecdotes), perspective (whose voice is centred?). Do they use similar techniques for different purposes? Or different techniques for similar purposes? A tabloid and broadsheet article on the same event will differ dramatically in language, structure, and emphasis — analysing these differences reveals how media shapes perception. MYP values critical media literacy.

flashcards.definition: In-depth, stylised exploration of a topic — blends reporting with narrative/descriptive elements.
flashcards.example: A magazine piece on climate refugees that combines statistics with personal stories and vivid description.

flashcards.definition: Opinion piece expressing a publication's stance on an issue — persuasive, often addresses current events.
flashcards.example: Newspaper editorial arguing for policy change, signed by the editorial board.

flashcards.definition: Preference/prejudice influencing presentation. Detect through: selection, framing, language, sources.
flashcards.example: Article quoting only one side = selection bias. 'Freedom fighters' vs 'terrorists' = framing bias.

flashcards.definition: Objective = fact-based, impartial. Subjective = influenced by personal feelings/opinions.
News structure: most important information first, then descending detail. Readers get key facts immediately.
flashcards.example: Lead: what happened, who, where, when. Then: how, why. Then: background, context, minor details.

flashcards.definition: Personal narrative focused on a specific theme, period, or relationship — not a full life story.
flashcards.example: A memoir about the author's year living in rural Japan — focuses on that experience, not entire life.

flashcards.definition: A key quotation from the article highlighted in larger text to attract attention.
flashcards.example: A striking sentence from an interview pulled out and displayed prominently in the article layout.

flashcards.definition: Using 'you' to speak directly to the reader — creates personal connection.
flashcards.example: 'You might think this doesn't affect you. But you would be wrong.'

flashcards.definition: Tabloid: sensationalist, short sentences, emotive, celebrity focus. Broadsheet: measured, detailed, serious news.
Informal, personal voice, often interactive (comments), regularly updated. Can be any topic.
flashcards.example: Travel blog: personal experiences, photos, tips — conversational tone.

flashcards.definition: Biography: life story written by someone else. Autobiography: life story written by the subject.
flashcards.example: A historian writing about Churchill = biography. Churchill writing his own story = autobiography.

flashcards.definition: Text accompanying an image, providing context or commentary.
